extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103 after KSR v. Teleflex, describing the factual inquiries, person of ordinary skill considerations, permissible rationales for obviousness, required articulations by examiners, and how to treat applicant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the scope and content of the prior art; ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must consider objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) when properly presented by applicants. Examiners act as fact finders when resolving these inquiries and must articulate findings as to scope and content of the prior art as necessary to support the obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner as fact-finder and articulation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners act as fact finders when resolving the Graham inquiries and must articulate findings as to the scope and content of the prior art as necessary to support the obviousness rejection being made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103, an examiner must articulate a reason or rationale to support the obviousness rejection. Examiners must resolve the Graham inquiries, articulate appropriate findings as identified by Examination Guidelines, and explain how the rationale leads to a conclusion of obviousness under §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale must be based on state of the art, not hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: In formulating a rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103, the rationale should be based on the state of the art and not on impermissible hindsight, e.g., applicant’s disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should avoid relying on the applicant's disclosure to supply a motivation to combine or other hindsight-based inferences. Clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious, grounded in prior art and common knowledge, is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for all claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners need to account for all claim limitations in their rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either indicate how each limitation is shown by the reference(s) applied, or provide an explanation. Each limitation must be addressed in the obviousness analysis rather than ignored or assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/scope of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is not limited to the references being applied; it includes both the specialized understanding of one of ordinary skill in the art, and the common understanding of the layman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may rely on, for example, official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity to support findings about what was known or obvious in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art — factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered in determining the level of ordinary skill in the art include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; (5) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel may additionally rely on their own technical expertise to describe the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill in the art. In re GPAC and KSR recognize this hypothetical person is of ordinary creativity, not an automaton, and may fit teachings of multiple patents together like puzzle pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill — creativity and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill in the art is also a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton, and may be able to fit teachings of multiple patents together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel (examiners and administrative patent judges) are persons of scientific competence and may inform findings by their scientific knowledge. Inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill would employ may be taken into account (cites: KSR; In re Berg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements by known methods (predictable results)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination would have yielded predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and each element would have performed the same function; (3) a finding that the results of the combination were predictable. Note caution: combining known prior art elements is not sufficient if the results would not have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — Simple substitution of known equivalent element
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because the substitution of one known element for another would have yielded predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device differing from the claimed device by substitution of components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — Use of known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because the technique for improving a particular class of devices was part of the ordinary capabilities of a person of ordinary skill in the art, in view of the teaching of the technique for improvement in other situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) the prior art contained a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention is an improvement; (2) the prior art contained a comparable device that was improved in the same way; (3) one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique to the base device and the results would have been predictable. Caution: if actual application would have been beyond the skill of one of ordinary skill, the resulting invention may not be obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because a particular known technique was recognized as part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) finding that prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) finding that prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; (3) finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — 'Obvious to try' (finite predictable solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because 'a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp. If this leads to the anticipated success, it is likely the product not of innovation but of ordinary skill and common sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) there had been a recognized problem or need in the art (including design need or market pressure); (2) there had been a finite number of identified predictable potential solutions; (3) one of ordinary skill could have pursued the known options with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same/different field
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because design incentives or market forces provided a reason to make an adaptation, and the invention resulted from application of prior knowledge in a predictable manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) prior art (same or different field) included a similar or analogous device; (2) design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; (3) differences between the claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or a principle known in the prior art; (4) one of ordinary skill, in view of incentives/forces, could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — Teaching-Suggestion-Motivation (TSM) test (permissible rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine the prior art to achieve the claimed invention and there would have been a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate: (1) there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation (in references or general knowledge) to modify or combine reference teachings; (2) there was a reasonable expectation of success. The Supreme Court stated TSM is one of a number of valid rationales and should not be applied rigidly or exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales list not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of rationales provided (A–G) is not intended to be all-inclusive; other rationales may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of which rationale is used, the key is clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant traverse requirement (37 CFR 1.111(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant traverses an obviousness rejection under § 103, a reasoned statement must be included explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings or the conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The traverse must be substantive — mere assertion is insufficient. Cite: 37 CFR 1.111(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of rebuttal evidence and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider all rebuttal evidence timely presented by the applicant, including secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner maintains the rejection after reweighing all evidence, he or she must clearly explain the reasons for doing so. Additional training on treating affidavits under 37 CFR 1.132 is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible reliance on official notice and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity when appropriate to support obviousness findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reliance still requires articulation and should not be a substitute for evidentiary support when evidence is necessary. The rationale must show how such common-sense inferences make the claimed invention obvious.
